questions.prompt: Explain why widgets do not run continuously in memory and how WidgetKit delivers timely updates in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that widgets terminate to protect device battery life and memory performance.
Explains that the widget extension produces a timeline of pre-rendered entries with future timestamps.
Explains that the system switches views at scheduled times without executing app code.

questions.modelAnswer: Widgets do not run continuously in device memory to protect battery life and system performance. Instead, an independent widget extension briefly launches to generate a timeline of pre-rendered entries with future timestamps. The iOS system caches these views and automatically updates the display when each timestamp arrives without executing app code. When new data is available, the host app or a push notification can trigger a timeline reload.

questions.prompt: Compare the three timeline reload policies (.atEnd, .after, and .never) in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that .atEnd requests a new timeline after the final entry date passes.
Explains that .after(Date) schedules a reload at or after a specific future timestamp.
Explains that .never relies on external reload triggers without scheduling automatic refreshes.

questions.modelAnswer: The .atEnd policy asks iOS to request a new timeline immediately after the final entry date in the current timeline has passed. The .after(Date) policy schedules a timeline reload at or after a specified future timestamp, which is ideal for predictable schedule intervals. The .never policy tells iOS not to schedule automatic reloads, keeping the last view active until an explicit reload is requested.

questions.prompt: Describe how interactive widgets work in iOS 17 using App Intents in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains that Button(intent:) executes AppIntent.perform() in the background extension process.
Notes that the action executes without launching the main application into the foreground.
Mentions mutating shared App Group storage and calling WidgetCenter reloadTimelines to update UI.

questions.modelAnswer: In iOS 17 and later, widgets support interactive buttons and toggles using SwiftUI views like Button(intent:). When the user taps a button, iOS executes the AppIntent perform method in the background widget extension process without launching the main application. The intent performs data mutations in shared App Group storage and calls reloadTimelines on WidgetCenter. The widget interface then refreshes immediately to show the new state.

questions.prompt: Explain why UserDefaults.standard fails to share data with a widget extension and describe the correct solution in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.description: Explains process isolation and separate sandboxed container directories between app and extension.
States that developers must enable the App Groups entitlement in Xcode for both targets.
Explains accessing shared preferences using UserDefaults(suiteName:) with the App Group identifier.

questions.modelAnswer: Widget extensions run in a separate sandboxed process with their own isolated file container. Accessing UserDefaults.standard from the widget reads a different preference file than the main app, causing missing data. To share data correctly, developers must enable the App Groups entitlement in Xcode for both targets. Both the app and widget then access the shared container using UserDefaults with a shared suite name.

questions.prompt: Describe the widget reload budget and how an architect prevents budget exhaustion in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.description: Explains that iOS limits daily reloads to 40-70 updates and throttles background calls when exhausted.
Recommends pre-generating multi-hour forecast timeline entries in advance.
Recommends using Text with timer style for live countdowns rather than triggering reloads.

questions.modelAnswer: iOS enforces a daily reload budget of forty to seventy background updates per widget to preserve battery life and device responsiveness. If an app requests reloads too frequently, iOS throttles background updates and ignores further reload requests. Architects prevent exhaustion by generating multi-hour forecast entries upfront in a single timeline rather than polling every few minutes. Furthermore, live countdowns should use Text with timer style instead of triggering timeline reloads.
